name: Mass Inflation Inside a Charged Black Hole
description: The inside of a charged black hole crossed by two streams of radiation, one falling in and one running outward. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel found in 1989 that the mass function then grows without limit at the inner horizon, which turns the Cauchy horizon of the Reissner-Nordström solution into a null curvature singularity, and Amos Ori gave the exact solution in 1991.
convention: We work in units with $G = c = 1$, so every coordinate with a dimension is a length, and so are the mass function $m$ and the charge radius $r_q$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Fall into a charged black hole and the mathematics offers you a way out. Inside the event horizon of the Reissner-Nordström solution lies a second horizon, and past it a timelike singularity that a traveller could steer around on the way to another universe [poisson1989, poisson1997]. Does anyone believe in that tunnel? Roger Penrose gave the reason for doubt in 1968: the inner horizon is a surface of infinite blueshift [penrose1968, brady1999]. It is also a Cauchy horizon, the edge of the region where data set at the collapse still fix what happens, and someone crossing it would see the whole future of the universe outside go by in a flash [poisson1989].¶The collapse itself supplies something to fall in: a star radiates its bumps away as it collapses and leaves a tail of radiation that dies off as an inverse power of time, Richard Price's law of 1972, and part of that tail showers into the hole [price1972, poisson1989]. When Michael Simpson and Penrose followed test fields into a Reissner-Nordström hole by computer in 1973, the fields grew without limit at the inner horizon [simpson1973]. But a test field leaves the geometry untouched [poisson1989]. The first step past that was William Hiscock's, in 1981, with the charged Vaidya metric, an exact solution in which a stream of light falls into the charged hole [hiscock1981charged, bonnor1970, brady1999]. A falling observer meets an energy density that diverges at the Cauchy horizon, yet the mass function $m(v)$ settles quietly to the final mass $m_0$ and every curvature scalar stays bounded [poisson1989, brady1999].¶Eric Poisson and Werner Israel, in Edmonton, added what was missing: a second stream, running outward inside the hole, for the radiation that leaves the star or scatters back off the curvature in there [poisson1989, brady1999]. They kept the hole spherical and charged, since its horizons are arranged much as Kerr's are, and let the two streams of light pass through each other without interacting [poisson1989]. The quantity to watch is the mass function $m$, the mass inside a sphere of radius $r$, defined by $1 - 2m/r + r_q^2/r^2 = g^{ab}\partial_a r\,\partial_b r$ [poisson1989]. Its source is the product of the two streams: in null coordinates, where the plane of radial motion has the metric $-2e^{2\sigma}du\,dv$, it obeys $\partial_u\partial_v m = e^{-2\sigma}L_{in}L_{out}/r$, with $L_{in}(v)$ and $L_{out}(u)$ the two luminosities, so one stream alone leaves $m$ in peace [poisson1989, bonanno1995]. With both, the blueshifted tail multiplies whatever flows outward, and near the Cauchy horizon the mass grows as $e^{\kappa v}(v/m_0)^{-12}$, with $\kappa$ the surface gravity of the inner horizon [poisson1989]. They named it mass inflation, and none of it shows outside, where the mass of the hole stays what it was [poisson1989, poisson1990].¶The idea came from a simpler picture: two thin shells of light, one falling in and one heading out, collide near a horizon, and the masses on the four sides of the collision are tied by a relation that Tevian Dray and Gerard 't Hooft, and I. H. Redmount, published in 1985 [dray1985shells, redmount1985]. Poisson and Israel wrote that it was through a generalized form of these relations that mass inflation "first suggested itself to us" [poisson1989]. The exact solution is Amos Ori's, built at Caltech in 1991 by keeping the influx continuous and squeezing the outflux into one thin shell, with a charged Vaidya metric on each side of it [ori1991inflation, bonanno1995]. Behind the shell the mass grows as $v^{-p}e^{\kappa v}$ for an influx that falls off as $v^{-p}$ [bonanno1995]. And the singularity is weak: the tidal forces diverge, but an object falling through is distorted only by a finite amount, so they "do not necessarily destroy physical objects which attempt to cross it" [ori1991inflation, brady1999].¶Is any of this more than a property of streams of light? A numerical answer came in 1995, when Patrick Brady and John Smith put a scalar field in place of the dust and integrated the field equations in an advanced time $v$ and the areal radius $r$, with two free functions of both [brady1995]. They found the null singularity of mass inflation along the Cauchy horizon, whose generators are slowly focused until it gives way to a spacelike singularity at $r = 0$ deep inside [brady1995]. Three years later Shahar Hod and Tsvi Piran followed a charged scalar field from regular initial data through the whole collapse and found the same two singularities [hod1998]. The proof is Mihalis Dafermos's, of 2005: for the spherical Einstein-Maxwell equations with a scalar field, the metric extends continuously across the Cauchy horizon while the mass blows up along it [dafermos2005].¶The rotating hole came next: in Ori's analysis of 1992 the perturbations of the metric inside a Kerr black hole stay finite and small at the Cauchy horizon while the curvature diverges, the same weak null singularity [ori1992]. For Poisson this is how general relativity keeps its predictive power inside a black hole in asymptotically flat space: the perturbations destroy the Cauchy horizon and put a null curvature singularity in its place [poisson1997]. A positive cosmological constant changes the outcome, since the tail then dies off exponentially, and where the surface gravity of the inner horizon is no greater than that of the cosmological horizon the Cauchy horizon is stable [brady1992, poisson1997].

related.text: The charged black hole with nothing falling in. With $m$ constant the ingoing chart is the Reissner-Nordström metric in advanced time, whose inner horizon is the Cauchy horizon that mass inflation makes singular [poisson1989].
The same stream of light with no charge on the hole. At $r_q = 0$ the ingoing chart is Vaidya's metric in advanced time, and William Bonnor and Vaidya gave the charged form in 1970 [bonnor1970].
The charged Vaidya metric with the charge free to change along with the mass. With the charge held constant its ingoing chart is the one each side of Ori's shell is written in [bonnor1970].
The rotating black hole, whose inner horizon the charged model was built to imitate. Amos Ori argued in 1992 that it carries the same weak null singularity [poisson1989, ori1992].

A regular black hole, with an inner horizon of its own. Raúl Carballo-Rubio and his collaborators carried Ori's shell over to it in 2021 and found the mass growing exponentially there too [carballorubio2021].
Another regular black hole with two horizons. Ori's shell gives it an exponentially growing mass at the inner one as well [carballorubio2021].

The charged hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. There the tail dies off exponentially, and Patrick Brady and Eric Poisson found in 1992 that the Cauchy horizon is stable where its surface gravity is no greater than the cosmological horizon's [brady1992, poisson1997].

The rotating black hole in three dimensions, which has an inner horizon too. J. S. F. Chan, K. C. K. Chan, and Robert Mann gave its charged form a Vaidya mass in 1996 and found the mass function diverging in the same way [chan1996].

Two colliding plane waves that end on the inner horizon of Kerr. Ulvi Yurtsever took such Cauchy horizons of plane symmetric spacetimes as a simpler model of the inner horizon of a black hole [yurtsever1993].

parameters.description: Mass function of advanced time, a length, $m = GM/c^2$; $m_0$ is the final mass in the drawings and $v_0$ the advanced time their tail begins at

Charge radius, $r_q^2 = Q^2 G/(4\pi\epsilon_0 c^4)$ for the charge $Q$; $r_\pm = m_0 \pm \sqrt{m_0^2 - r_q^2}$ are the horizons of the hole left behind and $\kappa = \sqrt{m_0^2 - r_q^2}/r_-^2$ the surface gravity of the inner one

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ constant along each ingoing radial light ray and $r$ the areal radius. The mass is a function $m(v)$, and behind an outgoing shell the chart has its own $v$ and its own $m(v)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Double Null

parameters.description: Areal radius, a function of the two null coordinates
Function that sets the metric of the plane of $u$ and $v$, a pure number

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, v, \theta, \phi)$, with $u$ and $v$ any two null coordinates on the plane of radial motion, both lengths and both growing toward the future. The mass function $m$ is defined by $1 - 2m/r + r_q^2/r^2 = -2e^{-2\sigma}\,\partial_u r\,\partial_v r$, and no component assumes a field equation. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
